title: Amazon KDP Guide for First-Time Authors
excerpt: Amazon KDP is the free self-publishing platform that puts your ebook or print book on Amazon without an agent, a publisher, or upfront fees. This guide explains how it works — royalties, file formats, publishing steps, and the most common first-timer mistakes to avoid.
meta_title: Amazon KDP Guide 2026 — How Kindle Direct Publishing Works

html:
KDP stands for Kindle Direct Publishing, Amazon's self-publishing platform. You upload your manuscript and cover, set a price, and sell your book on Amazon as an ebook, a paperback or a hardcover. Publishing is free; Amazon pays you a royalty on each sale. KDP says a new book takes about 3 business days to go live. No literary agent. No publisher. No upfront cost.

This guide explains how KDP works for first-time authors: ebook and paperback publishing, royalties, formatting, ISBNs, pricing, KDP Select, and the most common mistakes on a first upload. Every figure below is taken from KDP's own help pages.

What Is Amazon KDP and How Does It Work?

KDP stands for Kindle Direct Publishing. It's the self-publishing arm of Amazon, launched in 2007 alongside the original Kindle. What started as an ebook-only platform now supports paperback and hardcover print-on-demand books as well — meaning you can sell a physical book on Amazon without holding inventory.

KDP provides:

  • Global distribution — Your ebook appears in Amazon's Kindle Store in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, India, Germany, France, and more.
  • Free publishing — No upfront fees. KDP takes a percentage of sales.
  • Royalty payments — Amazon pays royalties monthly, approximately 60 days after the end of the month, once you meet the minimum payment threshold.
  • Full control — You set your price, keep the rights, and can update or unpublish at any time.

KDP is not a publisher. Amazon doesn't promote your book or guarantee sales. But it gives any author the infrastructure to sell globally from day one.

Ebook Publishing on KDP

Your ebook is listed in the Kindle Store and readable on Kindle devices, the Kindle app for iOS and Android, tablets, and computers. Amazon converts your uploaded file to Kindle format automatically.

The preferred upload format is EPUB. KDP also accepts DOCX and HTML, but EPUB gives you the most control over how your book looks inside the app. KDP also accepts KPF files made with Amazon's free Kindle Create tool. An EPUB that doesn't pass KDP's validator gets rejected — the most common first-time publishing problem, and the one most easily avoided with a pre-upload validation step.

Paperback Publishing on KDP

Your paperback or hardcover is printed only when a customer orders it. You never hold inventory. If your interior has images that bleed to the page edge, you must upload it as a PDF. Without bleed, KDP also accepts DOC, DOCX, RTF, HTML or TXT and converts the file to PDF. The cover is a single PDF (back, spine and front) sized for your trim size and page count, or you can build one with KDP's Cover Creator.

Each print format needs its own ISBN (see below). Deciding between ebook only and ebook plus paperback? The KDP print vs digital guide compares formats, royalties and distribution.

How KDP Royalties Work

Two royalty options for ebooks:

  • 70% royalty — For ebooks with a list price from $2.99 to $12.99 on Amazon.com. KDP raised the top of this band from $9.99 to $12.99 on July 7, 2026, with matching changes in other marketplaces. A delivery cost based on file size is subtracted first ($0.15 per MB on Amazon.com). A $4.99 ebook earns roughly $3.49 per sale before that delivery cost.
  • 35% royalty — Applies outside that price band, and to sales to customers outside KDP's 70% territories. In Brazil, Japan, Mexico and India, an ebook earns 70% only if it is enrolled in KDP Select and meets the price requirements there; otherwise it earns 35%.

Paperback royalty on Amazon.com is 60% of the list price at $9.99 or above, or 50% at $9.98 or below, minus the printing cost. A $12.99 paperback with a $3.50 printing cost earns approximately $4.29 per sale (0.60 × $12.99 − $3.50). Sales through Expanded Distribution earn 40% minus printing. Printing cost depends on trim size, page count, ink and marketplace; KDP's royalty calculator shows your exact figure before you publish.

Pricing Your KDP Book

Your ebook price decides your royalty option. To get 70% on Amazon.com, the list price must sit between $2.99 and $12.99. Below or above that, you earn 35%. The 35% option also has a minimum price that rises with file size. KDP lists the bands for every marketplace on its eBook List Price Requirements page.

For a paperback, the price decides the royalty rate (50% or 60% on Amazon.com), and the printing cost comes off the top. Run the numbers in KDP's royalty calculator before you pick a price. For strategy — launch pricing, genre norms and when to discount — see the KDP ebook pricing guide.

Do You Need an ISBN for KDP?

Not for an ebook. KDP says ISBNs are optional for ebooks, and Amazon identifies your Kindle edition with its own ASIN.

Paperbacks and hardcovers do need one, and each format needs its own ISBN. KDP offers a free ISBN for paperbacks and hardcovers. Two catches: a free KDP ISBN can only be used on KDP, and the imprint shows as "Independently published". If you want to publish the same edition elsewhere, or under your own imprint, buy your own ISBN.

What You Need Before Publishing

  • Finished, edited manuscript
  • Ebook cover image: JPEG or TIFF, under 50MB. KDP's ideal size is 2,560 × 1,600 pixels (height × width); the minimum is 1,000 × 625.
  • Book description (your Amazon product page blurb)
  • Up to 3 categories (chosen in KDP) and up to 7 keywords
  • Tax info and bank account for royalty payments

Formatting Your Book for KDP — Where Most Authors Get Stuck

The most common reason first-time KDP uploads fail is file formatting. Amazon's review process checks your EPUB against a set of technical requirements. If your file doesn't pass, KDP rejects it — sometimes with a specific error message, sometimes with a vague "the file cannot be processed" message that tells you nothing about what went wrong.

Common rejection reasons include:

  • Missing or malformed table of contents
  • EPUB package structure errors (missing OPF file, broken manifest)
  • XHTML files that don't validate
  • Images referenced in the HTML but not included in the EPUB package
  • Metadata errors (missing language, missing title)

These aren't obscure problems — they happen to authors who export directly from Word or convert with Calibre without checking the output. A pre-upload EPUB validation step catches all of these before Amazon sees your file.

The Publishing Process, Step by Step

  1. Create a KDP account at kdp.amazon.com using your Amazon account. Complete your tax information during setup.
  2. Start a new title — Click "Create" on the dashboard and choose Kindle ebook or Paperback/Hardcover.
  3. Enter book details — Title, author, description, categories, and keywords.
  4. Upload manuscript and cover — Use KDP's built-in previewer to check chapter breaks, the table of contents, and any images before proceeding.
  5. Set your price and royalty rate — KDP shows your estimated royalty per sale in real time.
  6. Publish — Ebooks go live in up to 3 business days. Paperback detail pages appear in up to 72 hours on Amazon.com and up to 5 days on other marketplaces.

After publishing, you can update your book's content, cover, or metadata at any time. Changes go through the same review, which can take up to 3 business days.

KDP Select: Is It Worth It?

During setup, KDP will ask whether you want to enroll in KDP Select. This is optional — and understanding it before you decide matters.

What KDP Select gives you:

  • Your book is included in Kindle Unlimited — Amazon's subscription service where readers pay a monthly fee to read as many books as they want. You earn a share of the monthly KDP Select Global Fund based on pages read (KENP). The per-page amount changes each month.
  • Access to promotional tools: up to 5 free promotion days per 90-day enrollment period, and Kindle Countdown Deals (Amazon.com and Amazon.co.uk only).
  • 70% royalties on sales in Brazil, Japan, Mexico and India, if your price meets the requirements there.

What KDP Select requires:

  • Exclusivity — While enrolled, the digital edition of your book can only be distributed through KDP. You cannot sell it on Apple Books, Kobo, Barnes & Noble, or anywhere else, including your own website. Your paperback is not affected.
  • 90-day enrollment periods — Enrollment runs in 90-day periods. Check your enrollment settings on your KDP Bookshelf before a period ends if you plan to leave.

KDP Select works well in genres with heavy Kindle Unlimited readership — romance, genre fiction, and some non-fiction. It works less well for authors with an established audience on other platforms. You can start without it and enroll later if you decide to try it.

Common Mistakes First-Time KDP Authors Make

  • Uploading a file that was never checked. Exports from Word or Calibre often carry TOC and package errors. Validate first, then preview in Kindle Previewer.
  • Using the wrong cover size or format. The ebook cover is a JPEG or TIFF, ideally 2,560 × 1,600 pixels. A print cover is a different file: one PDF with back, spine and front.
  • Pricing outside the 70% band by accident. On Amazon.com, an ebook priced below $2.99 or above $12.99 earns 35%.
  • Enrolling in KDP Select while selling the ebook elsewhere. Select requires digital exclusivity, including your own website.
  • Taking the free ISBN without reading the terms. A free KDP ISBN can only be used on KDP.
  • Fake headings and manual spacing. Bold text instead of heading styles, and extra Returns instead of page breaks, break the Kindle TOC and layout.

For the formatting side in more detail, see common Kindle formatting mistakes.

KDP vs. Traditional Publishing

KDPTraditional Publishing
Time to publishDaysOften a year or more
Royalty rate35% or 70% (ebook); 50% or 60% minus printing (paperback)A lower share of list price, set by contract
AdvanceNoneVaries by publisher and contract
Editorial supportSelf-arrangedIncluded
Physical bookstoresDifficultStandard
RightsYou keep themLicensed to publisher

The two paths aren't mutually exclusive. KDP is fastest and highest-margin — which matters most for authors in fast-moving genres or with an established platform.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to publish on Amazon KDP?

Publishing on KDP is free. There are no setup fees, no annual fees, and no fees to update your book. Amazon takes a percentage of sales — you only pay when you sell something.

How long does it take for a KDP book to go live?

Ebooks go live in up to 3 business days after you publish. Paperback detail pages appear in up to 72 hours on Amazon.com and up to 5 days on other marketplaces. If your file is rejected, the review clock restarts when you resubmit.

Can I sell my book elsewhere if I publish on KDP?

Yes, unless you're enrolled in KDP Select. Without KDP Select, you can sell the same ebook on Apple Books, Kobo, Barnes & Noble, Google Play, and your own website simultaneously.

What's the difference between KDP and Kindle Unlimited?

KDP is the publishing platform — how you get your book onto Amazon. Kindle Unlimited is a reader subscription service. Enrolling in KDP Select makes your book available in Kindle Unlimited. You can publish on KDP without enrolling in either KDP Select or Kindle Unlimited.

Why does KDP reject EPUB files?

The most common reasons are structural EPUB errors — a missing or malformed table of contents, broken OPF manifest, invalid XHTML, or image reference mismatches. Run your EPUB through a validator before uploading. See KDP rejecting your EPUB file for a full breakdown of causes and fixes.

Do I need an ISBN to publish on KDP?

Not for an ebook — KDP says ISBNs are optional for ebooks, and Amazon assigns its own ASIN. Paperbacks and hardcovers need an ISBN, one per format. KDP offers a free one for print books, but it can only be used on KDP. ISBNs are also needed if you want distribution through library catalogs, IngramSpark, or physical bookstore ordering systems.
